# Visual hierarchy

Source: *The UI/UX Playbook* (uxpeak). Each entry separates **what the PDF states** from **our interpretation of its images**. Text explanations are complete without the images. Back to the [index](../index.md).

<a id="vh-01"></a>
## VH-01 - Give actions a clear priority order

When several actions sit together, make the most important one visually dominant, the next one quieter, and the least important one quietest.

- **Source:** PDF 7 (printed 6), 8 (printed 7)
- **Applies when:** Groups of buttons or actions with different importance (e.g. Checkout vs Continue shopping vs Remove).

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- Visual hierarchy arranges elements to show their order of importance using size, colour, weight and position.
- If every action looks the same, nothing stands out; giving each action a different colour while keeping the same size and style still leaves importance unclear.
- In the corrected cart, Checkout is a vibrant filled button, Continue shopping is grey (same size), and Remove becomes a small red text link.

**Mistake:** All actions share one style (e.g. identical dark buttons), or they differ only by hue while sharing the same size and filled style.  
**Effect:** Users cannot tell which action is primary; the eye has no entry point.

**Correction:** Use a three-level treatment: filled, high-emphasis primary; neutral/low-emphasis secondary; text-link or minimal tertiary for minor or destructive item-level actions.  
**Why it works:** Emphasis differences in fill, colour and size map directly to importance.

**Observable checks:**
- Count filled, high-contrast buttons in each action group: more than one usually means unclear priority.
- Do minor per-item actions (Remove, Edit) look as heavy as the main flow action?
- Would a first-time user point to the same primary action you intend?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Related:** [CNS-02](11-consistency.md#cns-02), [COL-01](14-color.md#col-01), [VH-04](02-visual-hierarchy.md#vh-04)

<a id="vh-02"></a>
## VH-02 - Don't let unimportant content dominate

Low-priority elements (oversized images, minor attributes) must not outrank the information users actually need.

- **Source:** PDF 9 (printed 8)
- **Applies when:** Lists, cards and carts where images, metadata and key data compete for attention.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- Oversized product images steal the spotlight from name, price and quantity and throw off the balance.
- Even in a balanced layout, showing quantity in a larger, higher-contrast style than the product name or price is a hierarchy error.

**Mistake:** Images far larger than needed, or a secondary attribute (e.g. '1 piece') styled more prominently than name or price.  
**Effect:** Attention goes to the wrong element; scanning for key facts slows down.

**Correction:** Size supporting imagery to its role and give the most important data (name, price) the strongest typographic emphasis.  
**Why it works:** Emphasis should track the user's priorities.

**Observable checks:**
- Which element in each item is largest or highest-contrast? Is it the one users need most?
- Does imagery take more area than the information it supports without a reason (see LAY-01 for when large imagery is the point)?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- LAY-01: where imagery drives the decision (e.g. food), a large image can be the correct emphasis.

**Related:** [VH-03](02-visual-hierarchy.md#vh-03), [LAY-01](09-layout.md#lay-01), [SIM-01](07-simplicity.md#sim-01)

<a id="vh-03"></a>
## VH-03 - Rank information before styling it; emphasise values over labels

List the elements on a screen, rank them by importance to the user, then apply colour, size, position and contrast to match that ranking.

- **Source:** PDF 10 (printed 9)
- **Applies when:** Any screen, and especially metric/statistic cards where a label and a value compete.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- Before designing, list the features and rank them by their importance to the user; a common mistake is emphasising the wrong elements.
- On metric cards, a large title ('Earnings') with a small value is wrong; the value should be large and the label small.

**Mistake:** Labels or headings styled larger than the data they describe (e.g. big 'Earnings', small '$4,981.00').  
**Effect:** Users read the obvious label instead of the information they came for.

**Correction:** Make the value the dominant element and demote the label to small, quieter text.  
**Why it works:** The value is what changes and what users scan for; the label is context.

**Observable checks:**
- In each KPI/stat card, is the number larger and bolder than its label?
- Has an explicit importance ranking been written down before styling?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Interpretation (ours, not stated by the PDF):**
- The corrected cards also format 2121 as 2,121; the source does not comment on number formatting.

**Related:** [VH-02](02-visual-hierarchy.md#vh-02), [TYP-11](15-typography.md#typ-11)

<a id="vh-04"></a>
## VH-04 - Use colour darkness and vibrancy to signal importance

Darker colours draw attention and lighter colours recede; vibrant colours highlight what you want clicked.

- **Source:** PDF 11 (printed 10)
- **Applies when:** Title/body pairs, and highlighting interactive elements.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- Darker colours naturally signal importance; lighter colours recede.
- A grey title with black paragraph text undermines the title; a dark title with grey paragraph text gives correct hierarchy.
- Vibrant colours (e.g. a blue button) can highlight elements you want users to click.

**Mistake:** Heading lighter than body text.  
**Effect:** The heading loses its role; hierarchy reads backwards.

**Correction:** Make headings the darker colour and body text a lighter neutral.  
**Why it works:** Contrast against the background equals visual weight.

**Observable checks:**
- Is every heading darker (higher contrast) than the body text beneath it?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Related:** [TYP-07](15-typography.md#typ-07), [COL-01](14-color.md#col-01)

<a id="vh-05"></a>
## VH-05 - Differentiate information with size, weight, colour and icons

Replace monotonous label:value lists with a structure where key data is large and bold, attributes get icons, and status gets a badge.

- **Source:** PDF 12 (printed 11)
- **Applies when:** Detail cards (property, product, profile) with several attributes of different importance.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- A uniform list of labels and values is monotonous and hard to scan.
- Use font weight, size, colour and icons to differentiate information.

**Mistake:** Every attribute rendered as the same 'Label: value' row.  
**Effect:** Nothing stands out; users must read line by line.

**Correction:** Lead with the key fact (e.g. price, large and bold), add a status pill, put the title next, show the location with a pin icon, show compact attributes in a row with icons and bold numbers, and show the contact as avatar + name + phone.  
**Why it works:** Visual variety by importance creates scan paths.

**Observable checks:**
- Are there runs of three or more identical label:value rows that could be grouped or iconised?
- Is the single most decision-relevant fact the most prominent?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Source issues / ambiguity:**
- The two property cards show different prices (£1,273,279 vs £3,273,279); this appears to be a source inconsistency unrelated to the lesson.

**Related:** [VC-01](12-visual-cues.md#vc-01), [VH-03](02-visual-hierarchy.md#vh-03)
